CO2016B-GE-21.exp: The passage closes by saying a leader or despot 'will combine the function of the priesthood with its own temporal rule', and that 'an alliance may exist between the interests of political power and the priestly caste' — i.e. the priests gained political power by joining hands with despotic rulers.

CO2016B-GE-22.exp: The king refused to withdraw the death sentence but said 'he would, however, allow him to die the death of his choice'. The jester then exploited this by choosing to die of old age.

CO2016B-GE-23.exp: The passage says plainly of the insulting joke: 'He thought that the king would appreciate it. But he was wrong.' No old score or lesson to the courtiers is mentioned.

CO2016B-GE-24.exp: The opening lines state that 'He entertained everyone in the court with his sparkling wit and interesting jokes' and so 'became very popular'. Making fun of the courtiers (option a) offended them rather than winning popularity.

CO2016B-GE-25.exp: After the joke at his own expense, 'The king felt offended and highly insulted. He became wild with rage.' The courtiers' earlier humiliation never reached the king, so option (b) is not the trigger.

CO2016B-GE-26.exp: The passage says he 'became very popular as the favourite jester of the court. This made the jester arrogant and conceited' — the pronoun 'This' points to his popularity, not merely his joking ability.

CO2016B-GE-27.exp: The passage explains that 'none dared to complain against him to the king as he was the royal favorite' — the king's strong liking for the jester shielded him.

CO2016B-GE-28.exp: The passage ends by noting that most renewable systems need 'hundreds of square acres of useful land', but with wave energy devices 'space crunch can never be a serious problem' — hence a saving of useful land. It also calls them cost effective and pollution-free, ruling out (a) and (b).

CO2016B-GE-29.exp: The passage states 'Through these devices the mechanical energy of ocean waves is absorbed and converted into electrical energy'. Wind energy, transmission cost and risk to life are not mentioned at all.

CO2016B-GE-30.exp: The passage lists fixed Oscillating Water Column devices under land-based systems and floating OWC devices under offshore devices, and says both categories of device are applied to harness this energy — so both fixed and floating OWC devices are involved. Options (b) and (c) swap the two, and (d) contradicts the statement that potential depends on 'depth of water where they arise'.

CO2016B-GE-31.exp: The passage says wave power devices 'are highly modular, cost effective and easier to upgrade' than conventional stations, which directly contradicts the exorbitant-cost and great-space options.

CO2016B-GE-32.exp: This is the NOT-correct item: the passage says wave energy can supply huge amounts of electricity 'without cooling towers and pollution', so the claim that it adds to pollution like conventional stations is false. The other three are supported — the cooling-tower contrast, waves containing as much energy as the world now consumes, and 'period of waves' being a listed factor.

CO2016B-GE-33.exp: The subject is 'I', so the present perfect takes 'have not' — 'I haven't seen you for ages'. The present perfect with 'for ages' covers a period running up to now, which rules out the past perfect 'hadn't'.

CO2016B-GE-34.exp: 'What have you been doing lately?' is the present perfect continuous, formed with have + been + -ing, which suits an activity continuing up to the present.

CO2016B-GE-35.exp: 'Just' with a completed recent action takes the present perfect: 'I've just started'. 'I'm started' would be ungrammatical and 'I'd/I'll started' mismatch the participle.

CO2016B-GE-36.exp: A past continuous is needed for an activity in progress at a stated past time ('when we last met'), and 'were' is the only auxiliary that combines with 'working' here.

CO2016B-GE-37.exp: 'I had been working there' is the past perfect continuous — had + been + -ing — describing a stretch of work before the later point of getting fed up.

CO2016B-GE-38.exp: The past continuous 'were arguing' describes the ongoing action heard at that moment and agrees with the plural subject 'neighbours'. Bare 'arguing' has no auxiliary, and 'argues' is singular present.

CO2016B-GE-39.exp: After the auxiliary 'had' the past participle is required, and the participle of 'forget' is 'forgotten', not the past tense 'forgot'.

CO2016B-GE-40.exp: In a past-time sequence the earlier action takes the past perfect: 'I didn't want to go until I had taken a photo.' Present-tense 'has/have' would clash with 'didn't'.
